snip.t: This elevated pressure is due to a combination of increased pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), increased pulmonary blood flow, and/or increased left atrial pressure.
Rheumatic inflammation → fibrosis & commissural fusion → narrowed orifice → ↑ left‑atrial pressure → atrial dilation → atrial fibrillation → pulmonary hypertension → right‑heart strain.

Rheumatic inflammation leads to leaflet thickening, commissural fusion, and chordal shortening, producing a narrowed orifice that raises left‑atrial pressure and generates the characteristic opening snap and diastolic rumble.

LV diastolic compliance – collagen matrix, titin elasticity, relaxation‐dependent calcium re‑uptake: Impaired relaxation raises left‑atrial pressure → dyspnoea on exertion, PND; examiner will ask about “preserved EF but high LVEDP”.

snip.t: Venous return pathways (jugular veins, superior/inferior vena cava, hepatic veins): Elevated right‑atrial pressure transmits back to the jugular veins (raised JVP) and hepatic veins (congestive hepatomegaly).

snip.t: Jugular Venous Pressure (JVP): Elevated JVP indicates increased right atrial pressure, common in cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.

qs.q: What downstream systemic consequence directly arises from increased right atrial pressure caused by tricuspid stenosis?
o: Pulmonary venous congestion resulting in fine crackles and pulmonary edema
Systemic arterial hypertension with a wide pulse pressure and collapsing pulse
Systemic venous congestion leading to hepatomegaly, ascites, and edema
Left ventricular hypertrophy accompanied by a displaced hyperdynamic apex beat
qs.e: Increased right atrial pressure from impaired right ventricular filling causes systemic venous congestion, producing hepatomegaly, ascites, and edema. Pulmonary congestion is a feature of left-sided heart lesions.
